display.title: Saying a Brachah: Why We Pay Hashem for Our Food
display.summary_short: David buys a cupcake and asks why he must still say a brachah after paying for it. A visit to the baker and the farmer gives him the answer.
display.summary_long: Young David buys a cupcake at the bakery with a quarter from his father, and his father reminds him to say a brachah first. Eating without a brachah, his father explains, is like taking something from the Beis HaMikdash without permission, because the whole world belongs to Hashem, as Tehillim says. David asks a sharp question: he already paid for the cupcake, so why pay twice? His father takes him back to the bakery. The baker admits that he did not create the flour, oil, sugar and eggs; he is paid for his work. Then the farmer arrives with a delivery and explains that he only plants, waters and takes care of his fields, while Hashem makes everything grow. On the way home David's father sums it up: when we buy food we pay people for their work, but the food itself comes from Hashem, and the payment Hashem accepts is a brachah. The same is true of apples from the fruit store or a table from a carpenter.
display.lesson: Everything in the world belongs to Hashem. We pay people for their work, but we 'pay' Hashem for the food itself by saying a brachah before we eat.

sources_cited.note: 'LaHashem ha'aretz u'melo'ah': the whole world belongs to Hashem.

segments.title: David's cupcake and the brachah
segments.summary: David's father explains that eating without a brachah is like taking from Hashem's house, and David asks why he must pay twice.

segments.title: At the bakery: the baker and the farmer
segments.summary: The baker and the farmer each admit they are paid for their work, while Hashem makes the food itself.

segments.title: Paying Hashem with a brachah
segments.summary: David's father explains that a brachah is how we pay Hashem for the food He created.
